title: Photius and the brood of mockers of whom Mulligan was one, and Arius, warring his life long upon the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father, and Valentine, spurning Christ’s terrene body, and the subtle African heresiarch Sabellius who held that the Father was Himself His own Son.
html_source:
A list of early heretics.

Photius, while not a heretic in the usual sense, was deposed by the Fourth [Roman Catholic] Council of Constantinople (869-870) from his position as Patriarch of Constantinople, the head of the Eastern (today, Eastern Orthodox) Church. This was in part because he was a layman when he was appointed to the Patriarchate. This was the first council that was not recognized by both East and West, and an early indicator of the approaching 1054 schism.

Arius (256-336) believed that Jesus Christ was not of the same essence of God, and was only the first creation of the Father. His promulgation of this teaching was the impetus for the calling of the Council of Nicaea in 325, the very first ecumenical council.

Valentine, more commonly called Valentinus, lived from c.100-c.160, and was a Christian gnostic theologian who believed that the material world was evil, and to some extent denied the incarnation of Christ.

Sabellius (3rd century) was a Christian priest who taught that God was not three persons, but three manifestations of the same person.

Arius, Valentinus, and Sabellius all held anti-Trinitarian views that were rejected and condemned by orthodox Christianity.
